title: The Kabbalah ranking and its Shi'ur Qomah anchor
statement: The canon names the Kabbalah 'the book closest to the truth' and cites two stature figures — the creator's height of 236,000 parasangs and heels of 30 million — and both figures are genuinely attested in the Shi'ur Qomah tradition transmitted within the Hekhalot literature; the corpus reads the correspondence as the canon engaging a real and identifiable textual tradition, with the article's light-second gloss recorded as its interpretive development.

includes: The canonical statement, which is explicit: the closest-to-truth ranking and the two figures (TBWTT-5:51-54)

The attestation finding, which is verifiable: both figures exist in the Shi'ur Qomah tradition (the Measure of the Stature), older than the Kabbalah proper and transmitted in the Hekhalot corpus and Sefer Raziel
The identification of the canon's referent: 'the Kabbalah' as the canon uses it most plausibly designates this tradition-stream, since the cited figures live there
The corpus development, labelled: the light-second reading of the parasang figures, at the article's inferred strength
excludes: Any claim that the Shi'ur Qomah's own tradition intends physical measurement; its reception history (including Maimonidean rejection) is preserved, not overridden
Kabbalah as a unified book; the canon's phrasing is read toward its identifiable referent, not defended as bibliography
Numerological extension beyond the two cited figures
The truth of the ranking, which is canon-internal

source_references.locator: TBWTT-5:51-54 (the Kabbalah, the two parasang figures, the light-second gloss context; the closest-to-truth clause)
The stature measurements including the 236 myriads figure family and the heel measure the article verifies
The scholarly frame for the Hekhalot/Shi'ur Qomah transmission
The scholarly account of what 'Kabbalah' does and does not cover, against which the referent identification is read

alternatives.statement: The stature figures circulated widely enough in esoteric literature that citing them shows familiarity with popularizations, not engagement with the tradition.
The Shi'ur Qomah's measurements are liturgical-mystical hyperbole about incommensurability; reading them as data inverts their function.
The light-second reading retrofits modern units onto parasangs; the arithmetic coincidence is selection effect.
